opus-5.5.text:
Well, look at the economics. OpenAI is spending billions of dollars a year, on chips, on electricity, on talent, and the revenue just isn't anywhere close to covering it. They've raised enormous amounts of money at enormous valuations, and at some point investors want a return. So the question is: where does that return come from?

The honest answer is that large language models are becoming a commodity. There are a bunch of companies with roughly comparable models, the open-source models keep catching up, and prices per token keep falling. When your core product is commoditized, you have to find some other way to make money. And the most proven playbook in Silicon Valley for making money off hundreds of millions of users is advertising, and advertising at scale means surveillance. That's what Google did, that's what Facebook did.

What makes it worse in OpenAI's case is the kind of data they have. People don't just type search queries into ChatGPT. They tell it about their health problems, their relationships, their finances, their fears. They treat it like a therapist or a confidant. That's an incredibly intimate dataset, far more revealing than search history. And now they're talking about devices, memory features that remember everything about you, browsers, agents acting on your behalf. Every one of those is another channel for collecting information about you.

Then put that together with the persuasive power of these systems. A chatbot that knows you deeply and talks to you in a friendly, fluent way is a very effective tool for nudging people, whether it's toward a product or toward a point of view. That's the part that really worries me. It's not just targeted ads; it's potentially targeted influence.

And I don't think we should take reassurances at face value. OpenAI started as a nonprofit promising to benefit humanity and be open, and step by step it's become a very commercial, very closed company. Their governance has shifted, the safety commitments have softened. So when the financial pressure gets intense, and it will, I don't have a lot of faith that principle wins out over revenue. That's why I think we need regulation, real privacy law in particular, rather than relying on the goodwill of companies whose incentives point the other way.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, follow the money. OpenAI started as a nonprofit that was supposed to be about benefiting humanity, and now it's a company that has burned through an enormous amount of capital with no clear path to profitability from the products themselves. Training these models costs billions, running them costs billions, and subscriptions and API fees don't come close to covering that. So you have to ask: what business model actually pays for all this?

And the obvious answer, historically, is the one Google and Facebook landed on. You give people something they find useful, you collect vast amounts of data about them, and you monetize that through advertising and targeting. OpenAI already has hundreds of millions of people telling ChatGPT their most intimate thoughts, their health worries, their work problems, their relationships. That's a richer behavioral dataset than anything Google ever had from search queries. The temptation to use it is going to be immense, and shareholders, once you're structured as a for-profit, tend to insist on these things.

You can already see the hints. They've talked about ads. They've hired people from the ad world. They've gotten into deals around devices and persistent assistants that go with you everywhere. And remember, Sam Altman has a long track record of saying one thing and then quietly doing the opposite, whether it's about open sourcing, about safety, about the nonprofit structure. So when they say they won't go down that road, I don't find that reassuring.

I'm not saying it's inevitable. But if you look at the economic pressures, the data they're sitting on, and the governance that has repeatedly failed to constrain the leadership, surveillance capitalism isn't some paranoid fantasy. It's the default path unless something actively stops it. And right now, I don't see what that something is.

astra-6.text:
Well, look at the incentives. These systems are expensive to build and run, and you need some way to pay for them. Subscriptions are one possibility. Advertising is another, and once you go down that road, knowing more about your users becomes commercially valuable.

Now think about what people tell a chatbot. They ask about their relationships, their health, their financial worries. You potentially have something much more revealing than a search history. And the same system that learns those things can also influence what someone buys or what information they see.

That doesn’t establish that OpenAI has decided to pursue that model. But there’s an obvious economic pressure in that direction. My concern is that the incentive to monetize people’s attention and personal information can conflict with the promise of an assistant that acts in their interests.

sol-6.1.text:
My concern is the incentive structure. These systems are expensive to build and run, and if subscriptions don’t cover those costs, there’s pressure to find another source of revenue. Advertising is an obvious possibility, and advertising becomes more valuable when you know more about the person you’re trying to influence.

Now consider how much you might tell a conversational assistant: your worries, your relationships, what you’re thinking about buying. That could be an extraordinarily intimate source of data. If the same system that you trust for advice is also being optimized to sell you something, there’s a serious conflict of interest.

That doesn’t establish that OpenAI will take that route. But I think it’s a plausible commercial trajectory, and we should be asking what enforceable protections would prevent it.
